title: Case 2: Causal Trial Emulation
text: “Does an affordable first-line diabetes drug protect patients better than insulin, or are we comparing two completely different clinical populations?”

title: Case 2: Causal Trial Emulation
text:
The Situation
Clinicians need to evaluate whether starting Metformin monotherapy provides superior protection against microvascular complications (kidney and nerve damage) compared to starting Insulin.
In observational hospital data, doctors do not prescribe treatments by coin flip. Patients prescribed insulin are often significantly sicker and have longer histories of disease than those started on metformin.

title: Case 2: Causal Trial Emulation
text:
The Challenge
When we emulated a randomized trial using standard 1:1 propensity score caliper matching across 62 patients (47 Metformin vs 15 Insulin), the matching algorithm discarded every patient: * Matched Metformin: 0 * Matched Insulin: 0
An audit revealed an empirical positivity violation: * Charlson Comorbidity Index: Baseline difference of -4.15 SMD between groups. * Kidney Disease & Renal Impairment: Baseline difference of -2.71 SMD. Every single insulin patient had pre-existing renal disease, whereas early-stage metformin patients had preserved kidney function. * The two groups had almost zero overlap in treatment probability, causing strict caliper matching to reject the entire dataset.

title: Case 2: Causal Trial Emulation
text:
What We Built
Rather than forcing inappropriate comparisons, we adjusted the causal inference strategy using HADES CohortMethod and Cyclops: * Excluded treatment drugs from baseline covariate extraction to prevent statistical model leakage. * Evaluated 432 baseline clinical features using L1 regularized logistic regression. * Switched from rigid 1:1 matching to Propensity Score Stratification (5 balanced risk tiers), comparing patients only against peers within similar baseline comorbidity ranges.


Before: Naive 1:1 Caliper Matching

0 of 62 patients matched (100% data loss).
Causal model crashed due to zero common support.
Prescribing bias left unexplained to stakeholders.



After: Propensity Score Stratification

62 of 62 patients retained across 5 clinical tiers.
Quantified baseline comorbidity disparities for clinical leadership.
Robust estimation achieved despite narrow clinical overlap.





100% (62 / 62)


Patient Retention Preserved via Stratification

Statistical stratification preserved the entire study cohort for risk modeling without forcing false clinical equivalence.

title: Case 1: Architectural Federation
text: “How do we allow clinical analytics to run at scale across hospitals without wasting storage duplicating massive medical dictionaries?”

title: Case 1: Architectural Federation
text:
The Situation
To run OHDSI analytics, an engineering environment requires two core assets: clinical patient tables and the Athena medical vocabulary, a dictionary containing over 10 million concepts and ancestor relationships.
In institutional IT, copying gigabytes of vocabulary tables into every single study schema wastes storage and introduces version discrepancies.

title: Case 1: Architectural Federation
text:
The Challenge
We deployed an enterprise architecture in PostgreSQL separating patient data (cdm schema) from the shared vocabulary (vocab schema).
When standard HADES analytical packages ran, queries crashed immediately:
ERROR: relation "cdm.concept_ancestor" does not exist

The analytics packages internally assumed the vocabulary tables were stored directly inside the clinical schema. Copying the tables would have duplicated millions of rows across schemas.

title: Case 1: Architectural Federation
text:
What We Built
Instead of duplicating tables, we engineered a zero-cost schema federation layer using PostgreSQL relational views:

Created instant, read-only views inside cdm pointing directly to vocab.
Fully satisfied all HADES and ATLAS query templates without copying a single row.
Orchestrated the entire stack (PostgreSQL 16, ATLAS 2.13.0, and Broadsea Methods Library) via containerized Docker orchestration.



Before: Duplicate Storage & Crashes

10M+ duplicate dictionary rows required per research project.
Hardcoded join failures across decoupled schemas.
Risk of vocabulary version drift between studies.



After: Zero-Cost Federation

0 bytes of redundant dictionary storage.
100% compatibility across all HADES R and ATLAS queries.
Centralized, single-point vocabulary updates.





0 Bytes


Redundant Storage Overhead

All 10M+ vocabulary records and ancestor hierarchies were surfaced to the analytical engine without duplicate tables.

Case 3: Precision Oncology
text: “Can standard hospital databases track multi-year cancer progression, treatment lines, and gene mutations without losing clinical context?”

title: Case 3: Precision Oncology
text:
The Situation
Cancer care is non-linear and longitudinal. A patient diagnosed with Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) undergoes tumor biopsies, molecular genomic testing, lines of systemic therapy, and extended monitoring.
Traditional relational databases store these events as disconnected billing entries, obscuring clinical context like treatment line and duration.

title: Case 3: Precision Oncology
text:
The Challenge
Legacy health record models struggle with oncology because: 1. Diagnosis codes lack explicit beginning and end dates. 2. Treatment lines (first-line vs second-line) are not explicitly tracked. 3. Molecular alterations (EGFR, KRAS) often remain locked inside free-text pathology reports rather than standardized tables.

title: Case 3: Precision Oncology
text:
What We Built
We implemented the OMOP CDM v5.4 Oncology Extension and the mCODE framework: * Modeled disease courses and therapy windows using the cdm.episode table, establishing parent disease episodes and linked child first-line treatment regimen episodes. * Connected diagnosis encounters to episodes through the cdm.episode_event table. * Standardized actionable somatic mutations (EGFR L858R, KRAS G12C, and Wild-Type) in cdm.measurement using international ClinVar concepts. * Built survival pipelines calculating overall survival follow-up from initial diagnosis across genomic cohorts.


Before: Flat Encounter Rows

Diagnosis codes recorded without disease timelines.
Inability to programmatically identify lines of therapy.
Molecular testing decoupled from cancer outcomes.



After: Two-Tier Episode Hierarchy

28 structured episodes capturing disease and regimen durations.
Actionable ClinVar mutations linked to clinical timelines.
235.6 total patient-years tracked in survival analysis.





235.6 Years


Follow-Up Tracked Across Molecular Biomarkers

Patient journeys across EGFR mutated, KRAS mutated, and Wild-Type cohorts tracked cleanly through diagnosis-to-outcome pipelines.

title: Case 3: Precision Oncology
Health Data Reimagined: The OMOP CDM Architecture
text:
Clinical records live in hundreds of incompatible dialects across thousands of hospitals. By engineering an OMOP Common Data Model foundation, we turned disconnected patient records into reproducible clinical insights.
Lead Engineer: Harish Mohankumar | Platform: OMOP CDM v5.4, PostgreSQL 16, OHDSI ATLAS / WebAPI 2.13.0, HADES (R)

title: Health Data Reimagined: The OMOP CDM Architecture
text:
1. The Multi-Billion-Dollar Translation Problem
Every clinic, health system, and diagnostic laboratory records patient care differently.
When a clinician in Boston writes that a patient has “Type 2 Diabetes,” the electronic health record might store it as an internal billing code like ICD-10 E11.9. In London, the same condition is logged as an NHS read-code. In Munich, it lives inside an unstructured clinical narrative.
The raw data exists, but the systems cannot talk to each other.
When medical leaders need to answer an urgent question, such as “Does Medication A protect diabetic patients from kidney failure better than Medication B?” data engineers spend months per site manually cleaning files and reconciling custom tables. By the time results arrive, budgets are spent and clinical opportunities are lost.

title: Health Data Reimagined: The OMOP CDM Architecture
section: 2. The Solution: The Shipping Container Analogy
text:
2. The Solution: The Shipping Container Analogy
Before 1956, international shipping was slow, fragile, and inefficient. Goods arrived at ports in wooden barrels, woven sacks, and custom crates. Hundreds of dockworkers spent days unpacking and restowing cargo by hand for every unique ship hold.
Global trade changed forever with a single innovation: the intermodal shipping container.

It does not matter whether a container holds electronics, automotive parts, or fresh fruit. Because the dimensions, steel castings, and crane locking mechanisms are standardized worldwide, any ship can carry it, any crane can hoist it, and any train can haul it without opening the doors.

The OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) is that shipping container for health data.
Maintained by the international OHDSI (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics) open-science community, OMOP achieves two foundational goals:

Structural Standardization: Every patient, encounter, prescription, diagnosis, and lab result lives in the exact same table with identical column names, everywhere in the world.
Semantic Standardization: Messy local billing codes and proprietary brand names are mapped into a single, unambiguous concept ID. “Glucophage,” “Metformin Hydrochloride,” and international brand names all map to concept ID 1503297.

Raw Records: Hospital claims, doctor visits, and lab panels arrive in disparate formats.
ETL Cleansing: Data pipelines validate date chronologies, remove duplicates, and structure inputs.
Vocabulary Harmonization: Standard medical dictionaries (Athena) map raw strings to certified clinical concepts.
The OMOP Database: Data is persisted in a relational store (PostgreSQL) governed by standard integrity rules.
Reproducible Analytics: Standardized HADES statistical packages evaluate causal questions and safety metrics.

title: Health Data Reimagined: The OMOP CDM Architecture
text:
5. Business Payoff


Months to Hours


Time-to-Evidence Acceleration

Once health data is transformed to the OMOP CDM, running new epidemiological studies does not require custom SQL engineering. Validated network packages run in hours rather than months.


Collaborative Research Without Data Transfer: Institutions join international multi-center studies with millions of patient records without sharing sensitive patient-level rows, fully respecting GDPR and HIPAA boundaries.
Audit-Proof Data Governance: Automated validation via the OHDSI Data Quality Dashboard (DQD) enforces thousands of consistency, plausibility, and completeness checks.
Reusable Analytical Assets: Every trial emulation, cohort phenotype, and survival analysis script functions as version-controlled code that runs on future database refreshes automatically.

title: Plain-Language Glossary
text:
OMOP (Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership)
An international open data standard that defines a common schema and terminology mapping system for organizing health records worldwide.


CDM (Common Data Model)
A standardized database blueprint. Think of it as a universal filing system where patient demographics, drug exposures, and diagnoses live in the exact same tables across every hospital.


OHDSI (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics)
A global multi-stakeholder open-science community (spanning academia, industry, and healthcare systems) that maintains the OMOP CDM and develops open-source analytics tools.


ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)
The data engineering process of extracting records from hospital source databases, cleaning anomalies, and transforming them into the OMOP CDM standard structure.


Athena Vocabularies
The master medical dictionary system used by OMOP. It harmonizes over 10 million clinical codes from systems like SNOMED, RxNorm, LOINC, and ICD-10 into standard concept entries.


Concept ID
A unique integer identifying a precise medical idea. For example, concept ID 1503297 universally represents Metformin, regardless of how a local hospital recorded the prescription.


Propensity Score
A statistical value (from 0 to 1) representing a patient’s probability of receiving a specific treatment given their baseline health characteristics. Used to balance treatment arms in non-randomized observational data.


Positivity Violation
A circumstance in observational data where certain patient profiles have zero real-world probability of receiving a specific treatment (e.g., when a medication is strictly contraindicated for patients with renal disease). Recognizing positivity violations prevents biased or misleading causal comparisons.


Episode Tables (cdm.episode & cdm.episode_event)
Specialized tables in OMOP CDM v5.4 that organize individual hospital visits into continuous clinical episodes, such as disease progression timelines or chemotherapy lines of therapy.
